messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Since the chemical exposure two years ago, Hans Weber, a 76-year-old divorced hotel manager, has lived as if danger could leak back into the air at any moment. The incident happened in the hotel basement during a maintenance problem with industrial cleaning agents. He had gone down himself when staff reported a sharp odor spreading near the laundry and supply area. What he remembers comes in jagged sections rather than a single narrative: the sting in his nose and throat, the sudden confusion among the staff, someone shouting to get out, the burning chemical smell seeming to coat the inside of his mouth. At times there is no picture at all, only a wave of terror that arrives in full force, as if his body has been dropped back into that basement without warning. When he tries to think about what happened, he can still smell it. Those disconnected, sensory fragments have come to feel more convincing to him than any reassurance afterward, and he has come to believe that his body cannot be trusted, that it reacts before he can understand anything, and that bad things can happen to him without any way to stop them.

That sense of bodily betrayal now shapes how he moves through each day. Hans says his body has become an enemy of sorts, launching into alarm even when he knows, intellectually, that he is safe. Because he no longer trusts his own internal signals, he is on guard even at home, listening for changes in the hum of appliances, a bang from a neighbor’s apartment, or any unexpected sound that might mean some new hazard has begun. Loud or sudden noises make him immediately tense and watchful. He has narrowed the world to a few places that feel tolerable, mostly a chair in his living room and a small office space at the hotel away from the lower floors, and even there he does not fully relax. The more on edge he feels, the more the event seems to return in fragments: not a clear memory, but a bodily surge, the chemical odor, flashes of the basement, enough to make the threat feel current rather than past.

In the months after the exposure, he began trying to manage these episodes in practical ways that made sense to him at the time. When the emotional force of the event came over him without warning, he would turn on the television at high volume or play loud music to drown out both the silence and his own mind. If he noticed himself beginning to think about the basement or the smell, he would monitor his thoughts closely, checking whether he was “losing it,” scanning for any sign that he was going crazy. He also stopped going near the site of the exposure. As hotel manager, he still oversees operations, but he now arranges for others to handle anything involving the basement, laundry, or chemical storage rooms. Staff have noticed that he reroutes his path through the building and becomes visibly tense if a maintenance issue is mentioned near that area. His efforts to avoid and override the experience have not settled it; if anything, the need to keep watch over his mind and steer clear of the site has deepened his conviction that he is fragile, that his body will react uncontrollably if he lets down his guard.

At home the same pattern has tightened. A sudden clatter in the kitchen or an unexpected sound from outside can leave him acutely alert, and in that state the sensory traces of the exposure return more easily—the smell, the fear, the sense of being overcome before he can act. Each recurrence seems to confirm what he has come to believe: that his body will keep reacting as though the danger is present, and that he is fundamentally helpless to prevent this. Once he starts checking his own mind for signs of breakdown, he feels less in command, not more. He turns the volume up higher, keeps himself busy with noise, and avoids anything that might remind him of the basement, but these habits have made his world smaller. He spends less time circulating through the hotel he once ran with confidence, and at home he lives inside a narrow perimeter of places he judges safe.

Hans finally agreed to seek help after a recent incident at work, when a sharp cleaning smell from a cart in the hallway stopped him in place and left him shaken for the rest of the day, unable to trust what his body was doing. What frightens him most is not only the memory of the exposure itself, but the belief that he could be overtaken again from the inside, by a body and mind he no longer feels he can rely on. What he wants, cautiously but clearly, is to be able to move through his hotel and his home without treating every sound, sensation, or passing smell as the beginning of another disaster.
